segments.text: Hey friends, 99% of people think that discipline means waking up early every
morning, working very hard, and doing all the things that most people can’t do.
To be honest, yes, that **is** discipline—but only at a surface level.
Real discipline is something that only 1% of people truly understand,
and often, the person who understands real discipline is the same
one who is also able to do all the things the 99% do.
This is the type of discipline for which you don’t need motivation.
It’s the kind of discipline that keeps
you working even on your worst days, and only 1% of people truly understand it.
Today, with the help of an amazing book, I’m going to explain
this real discipline to you—and I won’t do it in a boring way.
I’m going to explain it to you in the form of a story, through
which you’ll learn seven lessons.
These seven things will show you what real discipline is and how you can apply it.
Once you understand this, in the new year, you’ll get ahead of 99% of people.
And if you want to keep learning such book insights in story format, make sure
to subscribe to the channel.
To make things a bit more interesting, I want you to guess
the seven lessons yourself as I tell the full story—I’ll reveal them to you at the
end. Those are the seven lessons, but if you figure out what the seven
lessons are **before** I reveal them, make sure to comment and let me know.
Let’s see who wins! Now, let’s start with the story.
A long time ago, there was a very talented king in a prosperous kingdom
who was smart, cared deeply about his people, and worked very hard.
Because of this, his kingdom became one of the best kingdoms of its time.
Now, this king had many ministers whom he always consulted.
Each minister was skilled in different areas.
For example, one minister was extremely intelligent, another was very hardworking.
But out of all of them, one minister was the king’s favorite.
That minister’s name was Daman, and Daman… The king didn’t like him
because he was very good at speaking or because he worked a lot.
The king liked Daman because he had a very special quality—**discipline**—which
not everyone possessed.
Daman was the kind of person who would work even when no one was watching.
He took even the smallest tasks seriously.
The king praised Daman’s discipline so much that the other ministers were very
jealous of him. Once, something happened—the
king had a very precious emerald, and it went missing.
Many ministers tried to find it and figure out where it had gone, but they couldn’t
find the gem. Even then, the king said, “I am confident that Daman will definitely
find it.” Hearing this, all the other ministers were very angry and irritated.
At one point, they even said to the king, “Your Majesty,
we also put in time, work hard, and are always available for you.
So why do you like him so much?” Then the king smiled and said,
“I will tell you when the time comes.” Time passed like this, and work continued.
Now, there
was a major road project underway in the kingdom that was almost complete.
The king then announced and
called all his ministers, selecting the three top ministers among them: one
who was very wise, one who was very hardworking, and one—Daman. Calling
these three, he said, “Look, we have a very big project, and it is now complete.
I want each of you to go to the road, inspect it, and then come back and report
to me.” The ministers saw this as a great opportunity to prove themselves.
First, the hardworking minister went. The road was very long,
but he decided to walk on foot, no matter how hot the sun was.
He carefully made a note of whether everything was even and properly done.
So he set off.
He inspected the entire road, and despite
the exhaustion under the scorching sun, the road seemed good to him.
But he noticed some large stones on one side of the road, which were
probably left behind by the workers.
There were also some paint cans and a little bit of trash.
The rest of the road was perfectly clean and polished.
So he returned
to the king and said, “Your Majesty, the road you built is excellent.
There’s just a little bit of trash
in one spot.” If you ignore that, the whole road is perfect.
Now, the king was impressed by the hardworking minister’s effort.
Then the second minister—the intelligent one—went.
Since the first minister took a lot of time and
the intelligent minister was, well, smart, he decided not to walk.
He took some soldiers with him and went by horse carriage so that the work could
be done quickly, and even if his attention wandered, he could still inspect
the road thoroughly. So he set off with his horse carriage and a few soldiers.
He inspected the
entire road and found not one, but **two** spots where trash had been left.
Some stones were also lying around, spoiling the beauty of the road.
The rest of it was fine.
After doing this, he felt a little proud that he had spotted things even
better than the hardworking minister did.
Then he returned. He tells the king that there are not one, but **two** spots
that need attention, which makes the king happy.
He says, “Ah, very good!
You noticed two places.” Then comes the third minister—Daman’s turn.
Daman goes to the road and eventually returns, but it takes him a very long time
to come back. Daman also comes and says, “Your Majesty, that’s correct.
There are two spots with trash along the road.” Now, the intelligent minister
laughs and says, “See, I told you—there were only two spots with trash.
So why did it take you so long?” The king also asks, “Yes,
Daman, why did it take you so much time to do the same work?”
Then Daman explained, “When I went there, I also saw two spots with trash.
First, I inspected the entire road carefully, and only after that
did I conclude that there were indeed two problematic spots.
Even though I didn’t have to, I personally went down at the first spot where there
were large stones, and with the help of the soldiers, I moved them aside and
cleared the trash myself.” At the second spot as well, I helped a
little, and with the soldiers’ assistance, we cleaned the entire road completely.
Now the road was perfectly polished and ready.
All that remained was for you to announce it and start using it.
And yes, one more thing—while I was clearing the trash, Your Majesty, I also
found **your
missing emerald**. Seeing this, the king was very happy and then said something.
But before I tell you what he said, I want to share something with you
all, friends—listen carefully.
Look, everything I am today, and whatever little control
I have over my life, it’s all because of **one thing: discipline**.
And to be honest, if you want to achieve anything big in life, **discipline is a
non-negotiable habit**. But the problem is that most people confuse
discipline with motivation—two or three days of enthusiasm, and then zero.

Now, let’s get back to the story.
When Daman returned and explained how he found the emerald, the king **revealed
that he had actually hidden the emerald himself**. He knew that Daman would
be the one to handle it because Daman was actually a **disciplined person**.
See, the other two ministers had gone before.
They noticed the problem, but **none of them handled it**.
Then the intelligent minister told the king, “But Your Majesty, I didn’t have the
proper tools and resources, so I didn’t do it.” “I thought
about cleaning it myself, but I didn’t do it,” said the intelligent minister.
The king smiled and said, “Yes, that’s true.” “But Daman also went.
He didn’t have the resources either, yet he worked himself and made others work
as well.
That’s why I trust Daman more.
And that’s why I give him the emerald as a reward.”
Look, friends, this story isn’t just
about a road—it teaches an important lesson about **discipline**.
With this book, I’ll now explain how the lessons were hidden in the story.
**Extreme ownership**: as written in the book, see—the first two
ministers also noticed the problem, but they didn’t change it.
Daman **made that problem his own** and fixed it.
And this is where the **crux of the system** starts.
What the 1% of people do is—they don’t blame others or just
explain things; they **take responsibility themselves** and get things done.
**Second lesson: No bad team, only bad leaders.** The first minister went alone.
He **did have resources**, but he didn’t use people.
Then the second minister went… He did use people, but he didn’t get the work done.
Daman, on the other hand, **used the people
he had, leveraged his position, worked himself, and made others work too**.
The second lesson is: **There’s no such thing as a bad team; often, there
are bad leaders.** If your leadership is weak, your team often won’t perform
well. **Third lesson: Ego is the enemy.**
The second minister had an excuse—“I didn’t have the
right tools.” But the third minister (Daman) had the mindset: “Even though I
don’t have the tools, I will get someone to do it or take care
of it myself later.” Ego often gives you comfort, but **discipline takes it away**.
**Fourth lesson: Self-command before control.** When Daman
went there, he repeatedly
**got down and climbed back up** just to inspect the road properly.
Because of this, he was extremely tired.
He also had an excuse—“This isn’t my job, why should I do it?” But even after
getting very tired, he decided, “No, this road belongs to **our kingdom**; there’s
no time to waste—let’s fix it now.” And this is the **crux of real discipline**:
often, you have to do things even when you don’t feel like doing them. **Fifth
lesson: Prioritize and execute.** See, Daman didn’t fix everything by himself.
He did **what he could** on his own and then got others to do the rest.
This is another important lesson of 1% discipline: **do what’s within your
control, and for what you can’t, get
help from others to get it done.**Sixth lesson: Stay in your lane.**
See, the king had not ordered anyone to **clean the road**.
He had only said to **inspect it**.But Daman, without
waiting for permission, took it upon himself and got the work done.
Because often, **discipline also means acting without supervision or approval**.
**Seventh lesson: Discipline creates freedom.**
When he did all this work, that’s why he got the emerald.
And that emerald wasn’t just about money—it was actually **freedom**.
Often, when you bring discipline into your life, you might feel like “my time
is being restricted”
or “I’m being limited.” But in reality, **discipline sets you free**.
It gives you more money, better health,
stronger relationships, and increases your happiness instead of reducing it.
That’s why the author
says the **seventh lesson of this book** is that **discipline gives you freedom**.
